credential: Free FUN MOOC digital badge after passing at least 5 modules with at least 50% on each module quiz
scope_notes: Twenty-hour, nine-module French political-philosophy course on Machiavelli, Arendt, Rousseau, Gramsci, Foucault, Locke, Hobbes, Spinoza, democracy, power, freedom and the state.
required_resources: Modern browser and free FUN MOOC account; no paid tools required

component_evidence.pedagogy: Short explanatory videos, module quizzes, selected bibliographies and open-ended forum questions create a clear concept-to-reflection loop.
component_evidence.depth: Nine modules and twenty hours provide substantial introductory-to-intermediate political-philosophy coverage without attempting a full history of political thought.
component_evidence.practice: Each module has a four-question quiz, and open questions encourage critical reflection and forum participation; practice is meaningful but not essay-intensive.
component_evidence.materials: Videos, quizzes, bibliographies and discussion prompts form a coherent current MOOC package.
component_evidence.currency: The current run is open from August 2026 to August 2027, so platform availability and contextual framing are current.
component_evidence.expertise: Edouard Delruelle is a University of Liège professor of political philosophy and philosophy of law.
component_evidence.accessibility: Free, no prerequisites, French-original, flexible and badge-bearing.

recommendation_rationale: A strong current French-language political-philosophy route with genuine assessment and reflection. It is less writing-intensive than MIT/Yale but much more current and accessible.

academic_credits: No academic credit for independent OCW learners
scope_notes: Undergraduate introduction to epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, logic, philosophy of mind, race/gender and meaning of life, with quizzes, presentation work and four substantial papers including a revision cycle.

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course explicitly aims to teach philosophical thinking, not just survey positions, through discussion, argument analysis and writing.
component_evidence.depth: It covers a broad set of perennial philosophical problems at genuine undergraduate depth.
component_evidence.practice: Frequent quizzes, oral presentation, three short papers, a rewrite and a 2,000–2,400-word final paper create exceptional writing-intensive practice.
component_evidence.materials: OCW exposes syllabus, readings, lecture handouts and assignment prompts; it is complete though less media-rich than lecture-video archives.
component_evidence.currency: Fall 2019 is recent enough for a slow-changing philosophy foundation, and the inclusion of race and gender keeps the framing comparatively contemporary.
component_evidence.expertise: Miriam Schoenfield is an MIT philosopher with expertise in epistemology and rationality.
component_evidence.accessibility: No prerequisites and fully open access, though dense readings and sustained writing make it academically demanding.

recommendation_rationale: The strongest general philosophy introduction in the current pool for learners willing to do serious reading and writing. It is unusually strong on active philosophical practice.

academic_credits: No academic credit for independent OCW learners
scope_notes: Rigorous undergraduate ethics course spanning metaethics, consequentialism, deontology, well-being, equality, moral responsibility and related debates through extensive notes and four writing assignments.

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course is organized around close argument reconstruction and sustained written evaluation of competing ethical theories.
component_evidence.depth: Substantial coverage of normative ethics and metaethical questions reaches well beyond introductory moral awareness.
component_evidence.practice: Three short papers plus a final paper produce strong analytical writing practice.
component_evidence.materials: OCW provides extensive lecture handouts and assignment prompts, though the archive is less media-rich than newer OCW courses.
component_evidence.currency: The core philosophical debates are stable; Fall 2009 age has limited conceptual impact, though newer applied examples are absent.
component_evidence.expertise: Julia Markovits is a specialist in moral philosophy and reasons/ethics.
component_evidence.accessibility: Fully open with no paid requirements, but dense readings and writing demands create academic friction.

recommendation_rationale: A strong rigorous ethics course with excellent writing practice. MIT 24.00 is the better broad starting point; this is stronger for focused normative ethics.

credential: Free Open University Statement of Participation
scope_notes: Fifteen-hour Level 2 course on competing definitions of politics, political actors, spaces of politics and contested political concepts.
required_resources: Browser; optional free OpenLearn account for completion recognition; downloadable formats available

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course builds around a deceptively simple question and uses contrasting definitions and examples to develop conceptual analysis.
component_evidence.depth: Fifteen hours gives a meaningful intermediate introduction to political concepts without becoming a full political-science survey.
component_evidence.practice: Embedded activities and reflective questions support concept application, but there is no strong formal assessment layer.
component_evidence.materials: OpenLearn provides structured text and multiple downloadable formats.
component_evidence.currency: The course was last updated in October 2019. The conceptual core remains valid, but contemporary political examples are dated.
component_evidence.expertise: The Open University has strong distance-learning and political-studies expertise.
component_evidence.accessibility: Free, self-paced, downloadable and low-friction with a free completion statement.

recommendation_rationale: A very accessible conceptual introduction to politics, but Saylor POLSC101 is much deeper and current, while the French FUN course offers stronger current assessment in political philosophy.

credential: Free Saylor course-completion certificate; optional ACE credit uses paid proctoring
academic_credits: ACE-recommended credit available only through optional paid proctoring
scope_notes: Twenty-nine-hour course covering meaning analysis, argument analysis, sentential logic, Venn diagrams, fallacies, scientific reasoning, strategic reasoning and creativity.
required_resources: Browser and free Saylor account for assessments/certificate

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course progresses from language and argument analysis into formal logic, scientific reasoning and strategic problem solving.
component_evidence.depth: Twenty-nine hours provides solid applied critical-thinking and logic breadth.
component_evidence.practice: Repeatable unit assessments and a free final exam provide regular structured checking.
component_evidence.materials: Saylor curates readings, lectures, videos and activities into a complete pathway.
component_evidence.currency: The current version was last modified on 2 October 2025.
component_evidence.expertise: Faculty-reviewed Saylor curriculum is credible, though named specialist faculty are less visible than MIT/Yale.
component_evidence.accessibility: Fully free, self-paced, certificate-bearing and mobile-accessible; optional ACE credit is separate.

recommendation_rationale: The strongest practical critical-thinking/logic route in the category for most learners because it is current, assessed and broadly transferable.

academic_credits: No academic credit verified for the free route
scope_notes: Large 111-hour political-science survey covering foundational concepts, political participation/public opinion, comparative politics, institutions, behavior and contemporary applied examples.

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course combines disciplinary concepts, classic thinkers and applied contemporary political examples in a broad cumulative survey.
component_evidence.depth: At 111 hours, it is the deepest general political-science route in the current category.
component_evidence.practice: End-of-unit assessments, practice exam and free final exam provide repeated self-checking.
component_evidence.materials: A large curated set of readings, lectures and videos supports the full survey.
component_evidence.currency: The syllabus was last modified on 3 October 2025, important for contemporary political examples.
component_evidence.expertise: Faculty-reviewed curriculum is credible though less instructor-specific than Yale.
component_evidence.accessibility: Fully free, self-paced, certificate-bearing and browser/mobile accessible.

recommendation_rationale: The strongest broad political-science foundation in the current pool by scope and currentness. Yale political philosophy is deeper on canonical theory; Saylor is much broader institutionally and behaviorally.

credential: No Open Yale Courses completion credential
academic_credits: No academic credit for independent learners
scope_notes: Full Yale introduction to Western political philosophy through Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Tocqueville, organized around polis, sovereignty, constitutional government and democracy.
required_resources: Browser; lecture media/transcripts and course files are open

component_evidence.pedagogy: Primary-text interpretation and recurring institutional questions give the course a coherent philosophical arc rather than a thinker-by-thinker summary.
component_evidence.depth: A full semester provides substantial close reading of major political philosophers.
component_evidence.practice: Three 5–7 page papers and a final exam create serious analytical writing practice.
component_evidence.materials: Complete lecture archive and syllabus support independent study, though public learner feedback is absent.
component_evidence.currency: Recorded in 2006, but the primary texts and core interpretive questions are stable; the main limitation is narrow canonical representation, not obsolescence.
component_evidence.expertise: Steven B. Smith is a senior Yale political theorist.
component_evidence.accessibility: Fully open, but dense classic texts and essay-style work raise the barrier.

recommendation_rationale: A strong canonical political-philosophy course with excellent primary-text depth. Its Western-canon concentration is a real scope limitation; pair it with more diverse contemporary political theory.

credential: Free Saylor course-completion certificate; optional ACE credit uses paid proctoring
academic_credits: ACE-recommended credit available only through optional paid proctoring
scope_notes: Fifty-hour moral and political philosophy course centered on justice, rights, markets, Kant, Rawls, virtue, human life and moral community, with classic and contemporary texts.

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course develops moral reasoning by applying competing ethical and political frameworks to difficult real-world questions.
component_evidence.depth: Fifty hours provides meaningful breadth across utilitarian, libertarian, contractualist, deontological and virtue-based traditions.
component_evidence.practice: Unit assessments and a free final exam provide regular checking and application.
component_evidence.materials: Curated readings, lectures and videos form a complete structured pathway.
component_evidence.currency: The syllabus was last modified on 2 October 2025.
component_evidence.expertise: Faculty-reviewed Saylor curriculum is credible, though less single-instructor coherent than Yale/MIT.

recommendation_rationale: A strong broad moral/political philosophy foundation with current maintenance and free assessment. Less textually deep than Yale but easier to complete independently.

scope_notes: Forty-nine-hour environmental ethics course covering ethical approaches/worldviews, intellectual history, environmental justice and environmental law in US/EU contexts.

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course moves from ethical frameworks into history, justice and legal/political application.
component_evidence.depth: Forty-nine hours gives substantial specialist coverage rather than a short applied-ethics survey.
component_evidence.practice: Unit assessments, practice exam and free final exam provide regular self-testing.
component_evidence.materials: Curated articles, lectures and videos create a coherent specialist path.
component_evidence.currency: Last modified 3 October 2025, which matters because the environmental-law/policy component changes over time.
component_evidence.expertise: Faculty-reviewed course design is sound though instructor-level specialist attribution is limited.
component_evidence.accessibility: Free, self-paced, certificate-bearing and requires no specialist tools.

recommendation_rationale: A substantial and current environmental-ethics specialization. Stronger than a generic ethics primer for this topic, though legal/policy examples should still be monitored over time.

credential: No Open Yale Courses completion credential
academic_credits: No academic credit for independent learners
scope_notes: Full literary-theory survey covering formalism, structuralism, semiotics, deconstruction, psychoanalysis, Frankfurt School, historicism, feminism, African-American criticism, postcolonial criticism, queer theory and institutional critique.
prerequisites: No formal prerequisite stated; substantial reading tolerance expected
required_resources: Browser and access to assigned texts where not freely reproduced

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course systematically builds a map of competing theoretical approaches and repeatedly connects abstract theory to reading practices.
component_evidence.depth: Twenty-six lectures cover an unusually broad range of literary theory traditions.
component_evidence.practice: Two 5–7 page papers plus a final examination provide substantial analytical practice.
component_evidence.materials: Complete lecture archive and syllabus are strong, although some assigned readings may require separate access.
component_evidence.currency: The theoretical traditions remain foundational; the main limitation is that post-2000 developments are underrepresented.
component_evidence.expertise: Paul H. Fry is a senior Yale literary scholar and experienced theory teacher.
component_evidence.accessibility: Open lecture materials help, but dense theory and external reading requirements create friction.

recommendation_rationale: One of the strongest free literary-theory surveys available. It remains foundational, but learners should add newer work beyond the course's historical endpoint.

credential: No Open Yale Courses completion credential
academic_credits: No academic credit for independent learners
scope_notes: Twenty-five-lecture course in modern poetry centered on Frost, Yeats, WWI poetry, Imagism, Pound, Eliot, Crane, Hughes, Williams, Moore, Stevens, Auden and Bishop, with close reading and critical interpretation.
required_resources: Browser plus access to assigned poetry collections where not reproduced

component_evidence.pedagogy: Close reading, historical context and multiple interpretive approaches are modelled consistently across the sequence.
component_evidence.depth: A full semester gives substantial author-by-author and movement-level depth.
component_evidence.practice: Informal exercises, a midterm, two papers and a final exam provide strong analytical practice.
component_evidence.materials: Complete lectures, syllabus and exam study material are available; some copyrighted poetry must be sourced separately.
component_evidence.currency: The literary objects are stable, so archive age has little effect on core learning value.
component_evidence.expertise: Langdon Hammer is a leading scholar of modern poetry.
component_evidence.accessibility: Open lectures are easy to access, but the course assumes comfort with advanced literary analysis and external texts.

recommendation_rationale: A high-quality deep course in modern poetry, especially strong for close-reading development. Its specialization makes it less universal than MIT 24.00 or Saylor critical thinking.

credential: No Open Yale Courses completion credential
academic_credits: No academic credit for independent learners
scope_notes: Twenty-four-lecture guided reading of Vita Nuova and the Divine Comedy in translation, integrating literary, theological, political and philosophical interpretation.
required_resources: Browser and access to a translation of Dante's texts

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course models sustained close reading across the whole Comedy, integrating form, theology, philosophy and politics.
component_evidence.depth: A full semester gives unusually deep single-author humanities coverage.
component_evidence.practice: Midterm, final and a roughly 3,000-word final paper create strong synthesis practice.
component_evidence.materials: Complete lecture archive, syllabus, exam resources and paper prompts support independent study.
component_evidence.currency: The object of study is stable and the scholarly framework remains useful; archive age is not a major concern.
component_evidence.expertise: Giuseppe Mazzotta is a leading Dante scholar and Sterling Professor Emeritus at Yale.
component_evidence.accessibility: No formal prerequisite, but the long text and interpretive density create meaningful workload.

recommendation_rationale: An exceptional specialist humanities course for learners prepared to read Dante seriously. High quality, but deliberately narrow in scope.

credential: No Open Yale Courses completion credential
academic_credits: No academic credit for independent learners
scope_notes: Academic historical-critical study of the Hebrew Bible in its Ancient Near Eastern context, using source, tradition, redaction, literary and canonical approaches.
required_resources: Browser plus access to primary texts/readings

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course explicitly teaches multiple scholarly methods and applies them to primary texts and historical context rather than devotional interpretation.
component_evidence.depth: A full university sequence develops substantial historical, literary and methodological depth.
component_evidence.practice: Midterm, final and an approximately 10-page interpretive paper provide strong analytical practice.
component_evidence.materials: Complete lectures, syllabus and exam resources are public; some readings must be sourced separately.
component_evidence.currency: Core historical-critical methods remain foundational, though some scholarship has advanced since the recording.
component_evidence.expertise: Christine Hayes is a distinguished Yale scholar of ancient Judaism and biblical studies.
component_evidence.accessibility: Open and non-devotional, but the long primary-text reading and scholarly vocabulary can be demanding.

recommendation_rationale: A rigorous academic Hebrew Bible introduction with strong methodological training. Best for learners seeking historical-critical study rather than devotional instruction.

academic_credits: No academic credit for independent learners
scope_notes: Historical-literary introduction to early Christianity and New Testament texts covering Greco-Roman/Jewish context, gospels, Acts, Paul, Johannine traditions, canon and early Christian conflict.
required_resources: Browser plus access to primary texts/readings

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course treats the New Testament historically and literarily, with explicit training in exegesis and interpretation.
component_evidence.depth: A full semester provides broad early-Christian and textual coverage.
component_evidence.practice: Two six-page papers plus an eight-page final paper create exceptionally strong writing and interpretive practice.
component_evidence.materials: Complete lecture archive and syllabus support self-study, though assigned books may require separate access.
component_evidence.currency: Historical-literary foundations remain valuable; later scholarship should supplement the archive.
component_evidence.expertise: Dale B. Martin is a senior scholar of New Testament and early Christianity.
component_evidence.accessibility: Open to beginners, but sustained primary-text reading and three long papers create significant workload.

recommendation_rationale: A particularly strong academic New Testament course because its writing/exegesis practice is unusually substantial. Best for historical-literary rather than confessional study.

academic_credits: No academic credit for independent learners
scope_notes: Foundational social-theory survey from Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu and Rousseau through Smith, Marx, Nietzsche, Freud, Weber and Durkheim.
required_resources: Browser and access to assigned readings

component_evidence.pedagogy: The course develops recurring questions about authority, freedom, class, capitalism, domination and social order across thinkers, making comparison central.
component_evidence.depth: A full university sequence provides substantial primary-theory depth.
component_evidence.practice: Three timed short-essay tests plus a 6–8 page essay require repeated argument synthesis.
component_evidence.materials: Complete lecture archive and syllabus support independent study, though original readings may require separate access.
component_evidence.currency: Foundational theory remains relevant; the archive's main limitation is lack of newer theoretical movements rather than invalidity.
component_evidence.expertise: Iván Szelényi is a major sociologist and social theorist with deep expertise in comparative social systems.
component_evidence.accessibility: Open and structured, but dense canonical readings and essay work create moderate friction.

recommendation_rationale: An excellent foundation in classical social theory with strong comparative structure. It should be supplemented by more recent and more globally diverse social theory.
